assessments.explanation: The paragraph states the applicant's arrival in Canada and refugee claim date.
The paragraph describes the applicant's claims of risk and persecution if returned to Malaysia.
The paragraph details the decisions of the RPD and RAD, and the applicant's judicial review application.
The paragraph states the application is allowed regarding the section 97 claim and issues with the RAD's review process.
The paragraph recounts the applicant's prior applications for permanent residence and humanitarian grounds.
The paragraph summarizes the RPD's credibility and factual findings about the applicant.
The paragraph states the RPD's conclusion that the delay in claiming protection was fatal to the claim.
The paragraph states the RPD's findings regarding the presumption of state protection and risk upon return.
The paragraph lists the applicant's arguments on appeal regarding errors by the RPD.
The paragraph discusses the RAD's consideration of the appropriate standard of review and its legal basis.
The paragraph explains the RAD's review of new evidence and its relevance and admissibility issues.
The paragraph states the RAD's overall conclusion that the RPD's decision was reasonable despite some unreasonable findings.
The paragraph states the RAD's conclusion that the nexus to political opinion was not reasonably established by the RPD.
The paragraph reports the RAD's finding that the link between opposition and political opinion was unsupported.
The paragraph notes the applicant could pay a fine, reducing the perceived risk of harm.
The paragraph states the RPD's finding that the applicant was not personally harassed by authorities was reasonable.
The paragraph summarizes the RAD's conclusion that the RPD erred in its treatment of evidence on political opinion and gangs.
The paragraph states the RAD's conclusion that the egregious delay finding was reasonable and unchallenged.
The paragraph states the RAD's finding that the risk to life and torture was reasonably not established.
The paragraph states the applicant's argument that the RAD erred in applying reasonableness as the standard of review.
The paragraph argues the RAD should have held an oral hearing and deferred to the RPD's credibility findings.
The paragraph claims the RAD erred in rejecting new evidence and relying on Raza, which is inapplicable here.
The paragraph suggests the RAD's conduct could be perceived as bias, affecting the fairness of the process.
The paragraph states the respondent's position that the reasonableness standard applies to the RAD's review of the RPD decision.
The paragraph asserts the RAD did not err in applying the reasonableness standard to questions of fact and law.
The paragraph states the respondent's view that the RAD's deference to the RPD's credibility findings was appropriate.
The paragraph argues the RAD reasonably rejected the new evidence based on the rules and the nature of the evidence.
The paragraph states the RAD's reasons for not accepting the new evidence, which did not address the core fear.
The paragraph notes the RAD's decision not to hold an oral hearing was reasonable given the evidence.
The paragraph states the respondent's position that there is no evidence of bias by the RAD.
The paragraph notes the RAD's confirmation of the egregious delay finding and the applicant's agreement.
The paragraph states that only the section 97 issues remain for consideration in the appeal and review.
The paragraph reviews recent case law supporting the application of correctness review to the RAD's choice of standard.
The paragraph states the Court's view that the RAD should apply reasonableness to its review of the RPD's law and credibility findings.
The paragraph affirms the Court's role to review the RAD's application of law and credibility findings under reasonableness.
The paragraph states that the reasonableness standard applies to the admissibility of new evidence before the RAD.
The paragraph states the respondent's position that the RAD did not err in its procedural approach and application of law.
The paragraph discusses jurisprudence on deference to the RPD's credibility findings and the level of review applicable to the RAD's role.
The paragraph states that the RAD erred in applying the reasonableness standard and in its judicial review approach.
The paragraph notes that the RAD lacked recent jurisprudence guidance at the time of the appeal.
The RAD analyzed evidence and found credibility findings were unreasonable, applying an independent review standard.
The credibility findings were not determinative of the section 96 claim and only issues related to section 97.
The RAD erred by not allowing the applicant to make submissions on credibility concerns that were not challenged by the applicant.
The Raza test should not automatically apply to subsection 110(4) determinations, as the context differs from that in Singh.
The RAD referred to Raza factors but misquoted the materiality factor and based its rejection on subsection 110(4) and Rule 33.
The application should be allowed due to the RAD's error in applying the reasonableness standard; the RAD should reconsider the new evidence.
Subsection 110(3) states the RAD proceeds without a hearing but may accept documentary evidence and written submissions.
Subsection 110(6) allows the RAD to hold a hearing if certain conditions regarding documentary evidence and credibility are met.
The applicant argues the RAD should have held an oral hearing to respond to credibility concerns not raised on appeal.
The Board's discretion to hold a hearing was not engaged because it relied on the RPD record, which was not central to the current decision.
The issue of whether the RAD should have allowed the applicant to respond to credibility concerns requires further consideration.
The Supreme Court's decision in Mian addresses appellate jurisdiction to raise new issues and relevant procedures, applicable beyond criminal law.
A new issue is one raising a different basis for error beyond the grounds of appeal, requiring prior notice to the parties.
The court concluded raising a new issue is rare and justified only to prevent injustice, considering record sufficiency and prejudice.
Discretion to raise new issues involves jurisdiction, record sufficiency, and avoiding procedural prejudice, with considerations outlined in Mian.
Parties should be notified and allowed to respond when a new issue is raised on appeal.
The principles from Mian should inform the RAD's approach to new issues, requiring notice and opportunity to respond.
The RAD should consider if credibility findings are new issues and if addressing them is necessary to avoid injustice.
The main issue was delay, not credibility; the RAD's negative credibility findings could impact future decisions.
Fundamental fairness requires parties to have an opportunity to respond to issues affecting them.
The Supreme Court outlined factors affecting procedural fairness, emphasizing context-specific application.
Parties should have some opportunity to respond to concerns, even if findings do not change the outcome.
Allegations of bias are serious and should be made cautiously and responsibly.
There is no record evidence suggesting bias by the RAD; its broader review was related to its appellate role.
